strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: America's private jet boom is built on tax breaks and public airports, Fortune finds, as global sales reach USD 40.3 billion
lead.standfirst: Private jets account for 7 per cent of flights handled by the Federal Aviation Administration but only 0.6 per cent of the taxes paid into the aviation fund.
lead.body:
Global private jet sales reached USD 40.3 billion in 2025, up nearly 24 per cent over five years and growing at an annual rate of about 4.7 per cent, according to figures cited in a Fortune investigation published on 1 October. The magazine estimates that around 256,000 people, 0.003 per cent of the world's population, make up the private jet class, holding some USD 31 trillion in wealth. The piece argues that the economics of that market rest heavily on public policy rather than on the owners alone.

The most important lever is tax. One Big Beautiful Bill restored 100 per cent bonus depreciation, allowing the full cost of an aircraft to be deducted in the year of purchase. Fortune calculates that a USD 40 million jet could cut a federal tax bill by as much as USD 14.8 million at the top 37 per cent rate. Eight American states offer full or near total sales tax exemptions on aircraft purchases, and Massachusetts alone is said to forgo USD 25.3 million a year through its exemption. Commercial passengers, by contrast, pay a 7.5 per cent federal tax on every ticket.

Public infrastructure completes the picture. Of USD 7.6 billion in federal Airport Infrastructure Grants, roughly USD 1.3 billion went to smaller airports that serve mainly private jets, with more than USD 1.1 billion directed at projects such as hangars and runway improvements. The National Business Aviation Association spent USD 3.4 million on lobbying across 2024 and 2025, and helped defeat a proposed 10 per cent luxury tax on aircraft priced above USD 500,000 in Washington state before it took effect. One chief executive quoted estimates that about half of private flights operate empty, a reminder of how much repositioning sits behind every departure.

For the households that fly, none of this changes the aircraft on the apron. For the people who run their travel, it is part of the background to scrutiny that may follow: public debate about private flying tends to resurface around fuel, emissions and tax, and families increasingly ask their teams to keep clean records of every sector, every empty leg and every guest.
lead.why: A concierge or house manager who arranges flights should understand how the family's aircraft is owned, taxed and used, because the paperwork behind each trip, from empty legs to guest manifests, is what the family will be asked to defend.

articles.title: North American family offices are turning optimistic, RBC and Campden Wealth find, in a survey of 155 offices with an average net worth of USD 2.25 billion
articles.body:
RBC and Campden Wealth published their 2026 North America Family Office Report on 2 October, drawing on 155 survey responses from single and multi family offices across the Americas. The families behind them range from USD 100 million to more than USD 10 billion in net worth, with an average operating net worth of about USD 2.25 billion. The central finding is a change of mood: families are described as raising their expectations and shifting from caution towards optimism.

The report frames its subjects as enterprising, holding what it calls a long term perspective and a position of patient capital. Its main themes are the great wealth transfer, the rapid creation of new wealth at the same time, the effect of technology on how offices operate, and the difficulty of balancing near term performance against succession planning across generations.

The full findings sit behind a subscription, and this edition therefore reports only what the publishers have made public. Even so, the direction is clear and consistent with the other large surveys of recent weeks: family offices are growing in confidence, growing in complexity and preparing for a handover between generations that will change who decides what.
articles.why: Optimistic families tend to spend, hire and build, and a generational handover usually reshapes household routines, so those who serve them should expect new principals with new expectations.
articles.src: IREI, citing RBC and Campden Wealth

articles.title: Hong Kong's autumn art auctions total HK$2 billion, up from HK$1.3 billion in spring, as Kusama works meet a cool reception
articles.body:
The autumn marquee sales in Hong Kong ran from 28 to 30 September and together reached about HK$2 billion, or USD 255.78 million, against HK$1.3 billion in the spring. Christie's made HK$956.5 million, up 17 per cent year on year, and reported a 30 per cent increase in young collectors among its new buyers. Sotheby's made HK$956 million, up 35 per cent on its March sales, with a 91 per cent sell through rate and five artist records.

The South China Morning Post described a disciplined market anchored by competitive depth for fresh to market works with strong provenance. Among the notable lots, Leonard Tsuguharu Foujita's 1932 painting Chatte et chaton was sold at Sotheby's on 28 September. Works by Yayoi Kusama, long a reliable draw in the region, received what the newspaper called a cool reception.

The lesson for a collector's household is that buyers are discriminating: provenance and freshness matter more than a famous name. That has practical consequences for those who look after collections, because documentation, condition reports and clean ownership histories are what support value when a work comes to market.
articles.why: A house manager who looks after a collection should keep provenance files, condition reports and insurance valuations in order, since in a selective market it is the paperwork that protects a work's value.

articles.title: Fine wine has not been this cheap since 2014, Liv-ex says, as trade rises by a third and mature Bordeaux draws buyers
articles.body:
The Liv-ex Fine Wine 1000 index has returned to its 2020 lows and to 2015 price levels, according to a September analysis in The Drinks Business. Prices are down roughly 40 per cent in real terms since 2022 and have halved relative to the FTSE index over the same period. Liv-ex chief James Miles said wine has not been cheaper since 2014, and added that prices bottomed out around this time last year, with supply and demand now at more normal levels. Trade is up by about a third compared with 2025.

The opportunity, analysts say, lies in mature Bordeaux. Early 2000s vintages are entering their drinking windows at 2015 prices, and Lafite 2000 is at its cheapest in 18 years. Wines from 2006 to 2010 show a healthy bid to offer ratio of 1.7, against 0.7 for wines from after 2020. Miles said it feels like a good time to start buying again, while cautioning against expecting a new bull run soon. Another analyst, Sophia Gilmour, noted that the longer term upward trendline has been broken.

Selectivity is the consistent advice: back vintage Bordeaux and top classified Burgundy, liquid and easy to trade, rather than emerging regions.
articles.why: Whoever manages a family's cellar needs to read the market as well as the cellar book: knowing which bottles are entering their drinking windows, and which are liquid, informs both what is served and what is bought.

briefs.t: Embraer delivers 41 jets in the quarter
briefs.b: Embraer delivered 41 executive jets in the third quarter of 2026, split nearly evenly between its light and midsize models. The manufacturer says it remains on track to meet its full year forecast.

briefs.t: Cannes opens the boat show season
briefs.b: The 49th Cannes Yachting Festival ran from 8 to 13 September with 700 boats, including 117 superyachts and a brokerage fleet of 62 yachts with combined asking prices of about USD 640 million. Azimut's Grande 44M, at 43.85 metres, led the debuts.

briefs.t: A staffing market set to double
briefs.b: Cora Partners notes that the global luxury household staffing market is forecast to nearly double over the next decade, growing at about 6.6 per cent a year. Estate managers, senior chefs and senior butlers face the most acute shortages.
